name: Where to start a delivery loop
brief:
A van drives a fixed loop of `n` depots, from depot 0 to 1 and on to `n - 1`, then back to 0. At depot `i` it collects `fuel[i]` litres, and the leg from depot `i` to the next uses `burn[i]` litres. The tank starts empty and has no limit, and it must never run below zero on a leg.

Write `loop_start_depot(fuel, burn)`, which returns the smallest depot from which the van can drive the whole loop and return, or -1 if no depot works.

Example. For `fuel = [1, 5, 2, 4]` and `burn = [3, 2, 4, 1]`, starting at depot 1 leaves 3, 1, 4 and 2 litres after the four legs. Depot 0 fails on its first leg, so the answer is 1.
constraints: $1 \le n \le 200{,}000$; each `fuel[i]` and `burn[i]` is a whole number from 0 to $10^4$.
$O(n)$ time is the target. Driving the loop from every depot is $O(n^2)$.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: If the van starts at `s` and runs dry on the leg out of depot `i`, no depot from `s` to `i` can work either. Restart the count at `i + 1`.

examples.note: From depot 1 the tank never dips below zero; depot 0 is short on its first leg.
The loop burns 5 litres and only 4 are collected, so no start works.

tests.call: loop_start_depot([(i * 37) % 100 for i in range(200000)], [(i * 53 + 7) % 100 for i in range(200000)])
loop_start_depot([(i * 37) % 100 for i in range(200000)], [(i * 41 + 11) % 100 for i in range(200000)])

how: Submit runs 13 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value.
notes: Greedy choice with its proof: if a start at `s` runs dry leaving depot `i`, every depot between them was reached with fuel to spare. Starting at one of them is no better, so `i + 1` is the next candidate.
The loop works from some depot exactly when total fuel is at least total burn, so test that first; the restart rule then lands on the smallest working depot.
One pass over the depots is $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ memory.
